prompt: Why does an issue's number, like #12, matter to Git users?
hint: Think of a commit message that mentions it.

choices.text: Git uses it as the next commit's id
choices.why: Commit ids are hashes. The number belongs to the hosting service.

choices.text: Mentioning it links the change to the issue
choices.why: Right. The issue then collects every change made for it.

choices.text: It sets the order in which work is done
choices.why: Numbers are handed out in order of creation, not priority.

choices.text: It is the branch name Git requires
choices.why: Git requires nothing of branch names. Some teams include the number by habit.

prompt: On GitHub or GitLab, a pull request whose description says ___ #12 marks issue 12 as done when it is merged into the main branch.
hint: A verb, and it is the one this lesson used.

prompt: Which of these is the best issue title?
hint: It says what is wrong, and leaves the answer open.

choices.text: Fix index.html line 2 so it shows Sundays
choices.why: It names a solution before anybody has looked, and says nothing about the problem.

choices.text: Site
choices.why: Nobody could start work from that.

choices.text: Sunday hours missing from the home page
choices.why: Right. What is wrong, where, in one line.

choices.text: URGENT!!! Please look at this today
choices.why: Urgency is a label. The title has to say what the issue is.

prompt: Bruno opens an issue saying rye bread is missing from the menu. It was removed on purpose until the flour arrives. What should happen to the issue?
hint: An issue is not a promise.

choices.text: Leave it open until the flour arrives, with nobody on it
choices.why: An open issue nobody will work on reads as forgotten work.

choices.text: Close it, saying it was deliberate and why
choices.why: Right. Closing without a change is legitimate, with the reason written down.

choices.text: Put rye back, since an issue was opened
choices.why: The issue is a report, not an instruction; the decision stands.

choices.text: Delete it so the list stays tidy
choices.why: Deleting loses the question and its answer, which the next person will ask again.

prompt: What is a pull request, in Git terms?
hint: Nothing new is stored in Git.

choices.text: A special kind of commit
choices.why: No commit is made by opening one.

choices.text: A copy of the repository for review
choices.why: Nothing is copied; the page reads an existing branch.

choices.text: A merge request for a branch
choices.why: Right. With a page to discuss it first. GitLab calls it a merge request, which says exactly that.

choices.text: A command, git pull, run by the reviewer
choices.why: Despite the name, it is not the git pull of lesson 7.

prompt: What does git log --oneline main..sunday-hours list?
hint: It is the commits tab of the pull request.

choices.text: Every commit on main and on sunday-hours
choices.why: It lists a difference, not a union.

choices.text: Commits on the branch but not on main
choices.why: Right. What merging would bring in.

choices.text: The commits on main made since the branch
choices.why: That would be sunday-hours..main, the other way round.

choices.text: The commits that conflict between them
choices.why: It knows nothing about conflicts.

prompt: Why does the files-changed tab compare with main...sunday-hours, three dots, rather than main as it is today?

choices.text: Three dots is faster for large repositories
choices.why: Speed is not the point; what is compared is.

choices.text: It shows only what the branch changed
choices.why: Right. Compared with where it left main, so Bruno's commit is not in it.

choices.text: It hides changes that would conflict
choices.why: Nothing is hidden; unrelated changes on main were never part of it.

choices.text: main as it is today cannot be compared
choices.why: It can; it just answers a different question.

prompt: A reviewer asks for a change. Ana commits it on the same branch and pushes. What happens to the pull request?
hint: The page reads the branch as it is now.

choices.text: It shows the new commit
choices.why: Right. Same pull request, same conversation.

choices.text: She has to open a new pull request
choices.why: The pull request follows the branch; no new one is needed.

choices.text: The push is refused while the review is open
choices.why: Pushing during review is the normal way to answer it.

choices.text: The earlier review comments are deleted
choices.why: They stay, marked as outdated where the line changed.

prompt: Match each review verdict to what it says.
hint: One description is not a verdict.

pairs.right: This can be merged as it is
This should not be merged until something is addressed

right_distractors: Merge it now, skipping the checks

prompt: main is protected, requiring one approval and passing checks. Where does that rule live?

choices.text: In the .git directory of every clone
choices.why: A clone has none of these rules.

choices.text: In the settings of the hosting service
choices.why: Right. Git knows nothing about it; the server enforces it.

choices.text: In ~/.gitconfig on each developer's machine
choices.why: That file holds personal settings, and anyone can edit their own.

choices.text: In the commit history of main
choices.why: Commits record changes to files, not repository rules.

prompt: A reviewer commented on line 2 of index.html. Ana then pushed a commit that changes that line. What does the platform do with the comment?

choices.text: Deletes it, since the line it was about is gone
choices.why: Deleting it would lose the reason for the change.

choices.text: Moves it to the new line automatically
choices.why: It cannot know the new line means the same thing.

choices.text: Keeps it, marked as outdated
choices.why: Right. The thread survives, and it is clear it was about an older version.

choices.text: Blocks the push until the comment is resolved
choices.why: Pushing is how comments get answered.

prompt: The file that names who must review changes to each part of the code is called ___.
hint: Its name says whose code it is.

prompt: What did git merge --squash sunday-hours do before Ana committed?
hint: Read its two lines of output.

choices.text: Staged it all as one change
choices.why: Right. All of the branch's changes. No commit, and no record that a branch was merged.

choices.text: Made a merge commit with two parents
choices.why: That is the first button. Squash makes no merge commit.

choices.text: Replayed the three commits on main
choices.why: That is rebase. Squash keeps none of the three.

choices.text: Deleted the sunday-hours branch
choices.why: The branch is untouched until somebody deletes it.

prompt: Match each merge button to the history it leaves on main.

pairs.right: The branch's commits, plus a commit joining them
One new commit with all the changes
The branch's commits in a straight line, with new ids

right_distractors: Main unchanged until the next push

prompt: A pull request fixed a price, renamed a page and changed a colour, and it was squashed. A week later only the colour needs undoing. What is harder than it would have been?
hint: git revert takes a whole commit.

choices.text: Finding the pull request
choices.why: The squashed commit carries its number.

choices.text: Reverting only the colour
choices.why: Right. The three changes are one commit now, and revert undoes whole commits.

choices.text: Seeing who approved it
choices.why: The approval is recorded on the pull request either way.

choices.text: Pushing the fix, since main is protected
choices.why: The fix goes through a pull request like any other change.

prompt: After merging, the service offers to delete the branch. Is anything lost?

choices.text: No; its changes are in main
choices.why: Right. Only a name goes.

choices.text: Yes, the pull request page
choices.why: The pull request stays, closed and readable.

choices.text: Yes, the review comments
choices.why: They belong to the pull request, which stays.

choices.text: Yes, unless it was squashed
choices.why: Whatever the button, the changes reached main.

prompt: Put the life of a pull request in order.
hint: Review can loop; merge happens once.
items: Open the pull request into main
Checks run and a reviewer approves
trap: A branch deleted before the merge takes the pull request's changes with it.

prompt: Which of these are features of the hosting service rather than of Git? Choose all that apply.
hint: Would a clone on your laptop have it?

choices.text: Requiring an approval before merging
choices.why: Yes. A protected-branch setting on the server.

choices.text: A merge commit with two parents
choices.why: That is Git itself, lesson 5.

choices.text: Closing issue 12 when a pull request says Closes #12
choices.why: Yes. Git has no issues at all.

choices.text: Comments attached to a line of a diff
choices.why: Yes. Git records no comments.

choices.text: Squashing several commits into one
choices.why: Git does that with merge --squash, as the capture showed.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer an issue to a chat message for "add Sunday hours"?

choices.text: Chat messages are private
choices.why: Privacy is not the argument; permanence and linking are.

choices.text: An issue gets done faster
choices.why: Nothing about an issue makes the work faster.

choices.text: Git refuses commits without an issue
choices.why: Git has never heard of issues.

choices.text: It keeps request, decision and change linked
choices.why: Right. A year later the reason can still be found.
